before.content_html:
Why Every Cell Needs Energy

In the final metres of a 400-metre race, a runner’s muscles begin to burn. Oxygen can no longer be delivered fast enough to sustain the pace, and a different energy pathway kicks in — one that works without oxygen but produces a painful build-up of lactic acid. This is cellular respiration at its limits. But respiration is not just for athletes: it happens continuously in every cell of every living organism, from bacteria to blue whales, twenty-four hours a day.

The energy transferred by respiration powers all life processes: muscle contraction, nerve impulse transmission, active transport across membranes, protein synthesis and cell division. This energy is stored in a molecule called ATP, which acts as the cell’s immediate energy currency. Respiration is exothermic — it releases energy to the surroundings, which is why your body stays warm even on a cold day.

Key Fact

Cellular respiration is NOT breathing. Respiration is an exothermic chemical reaction inside every living cell that transfers energy from glucose to ATP. Breathing (ventilation) is the physical movement of air in and out of the lungs.

Aerobic Respiration

Aerobic respiration uses oxygen and takes place in the mitochondria. It completely breaks down glucose and produces a large yield of ATP, making it the most efficient form of respiration. The word equation is:

$$\text{glucose} + \text{oxygen} \rightarrow \text{carbon dioxide} + \text{water} + \text{energy (ATP)}$$

The balanced symbol equation: \(C_6H_{12}O_6 + 6O_2 \rightarrow 6CO_2 + 6H_2O\)

Because glucose is completely broken down, aerobic respiration extracts the maximum possible ATP from each glucose molecule. This is why cells with high energy demands — such as muscle cells, liver cells and sperm cells — contain large numbers of mitochondria. The folded inner membranes of the mitochondria (cristae) increase the surface area available for respiration reactions.

Anaerobic Respiration

Anaerobic respiration occurs when oxygen supply is insufficient — for example, during intense exercise, or in waterlogged soil. Unlike aerobic respiration, it takes place in the cytoplasm and produces far less ATP because glucose is only partially broken down. The products depend on the type of organism.

In animal cells (and some bacteria), glucose is partially broken down to produce lactic acid:
\(\text{glucose} \rightarrow \text{lactic acid}\)

Lactic acid builds up in muscles during intense exercise, lowering pH and interfering with enzyme function — causing the burning sensation and fatigue athletes experience. After exercise stops, you continue to breathe deeply to supply the extra oxygen needed to convert accumulated lactic acid back to glucose (in the liver). This extra oxygen requirement is called the oxygen debt (or excess post-exercise oxygen consumption).

In yeast and plant cells, anaerobic respiration produces ethanol and carbon dioxide:
\(\text{glucose} \rightarrow \text{ethanol} + \text{carbon dioxide}\)

This process is called fermentation. It has important commercial applications. In brewing and wine-making, yeast ferments sugar in fruit juice or malt to produce ethanol. In bread-making, yeast ferments sugars in dough, and the CO\(_2\) produced forms bubbles that make the bread rise. The ethanol evaporates during baking.

Key Fact

Aerobic respiration (with oxygen, mitochondria): high ATP yield, products are CO\(_2\) + water. Anaerobic in animals (no oxygen, cytoplasm): low ATP, product is lactic acid. Anaerobic in yeast/plants: low ATP, products are ethanol + CO\(_2\).

Respiration During and After Exercise

During exercise, muscle cells need more energy so the rate of respiration increases. The body responds by increasing heart rate (to pump more oxygenated blood to muscles), increasing breathing rate and depth (to take in more O\(_2\) and remove more CO\(_2\)), and breaking down glycogen stores in muscles and the liver into glucose. If exercise is intense enough that oxygen cannot be supplied fast enough, muscles switch to anaerobic respiration, producing lactic acid. The oxygen debt is repaid after exercise as lactic acid is oxidised to CO\(_2\) and water in the liver.

You can detect the products of respiration experimentally. Breathing out through limewater turns it milky, confirming CO\(_2\) production. Placing a temperature probe in a sealed flask with germinating seeds shows a temperature increase over time, confirming that respiration is exothermic. The rate can be measured by monitoring CO\(_2\) output using a carbon dioxide sensor or pH indicator solution.

When interpreting data from these experiments, consider: whether the change observed could have another cause (a confounding variable), whether the results are repeatable, and whether a control is needed (e.g. dead seeds in a sealed flask) to confirm that any heat or gas is coming from the biological process and not a chemical contaminant.

Key Fact

The oxygen debt is the extra oxygen needed after exercise to break down lactic acid built up during anaerobic respiration. It is repaid by continued heavy breathing after exercise stops. Lactic acid is converted back to glucose in the liver.

Growth Through Cell Division

A human being begins as a single fertilised cell no wider than a human hair. Over the following nine months, that cell divides billions of times, eventually producing the trillions of specialised cells that form a newborn baby. The key question in developmental biology is not just how cells divide, but how they become so different from one another — a liver cell, a neuron and a skin cell all contain identical DNA, yet they look and behave completely differently.

Mitosis is the form of cell division responsible for growth and repair in multicellular organisms. Before mitosis begins, during a phase called S phase, the cell’s DNA replicates so that every chromosome is copied. Then during mitosis itself, the copies are separated and two genetically identical daughter cells are produced, each with the same number of chromosomes as the parent. It is crucial to understand that DNA replication happens before mitosis starts, not during it.

Key Fact

DNA replication occurs during S phase, before mitosis begins — not during mitosis itself. Mitosis then separates the copied chromosomes to produce two genetically identical daughter cells with the same chromosome number as the parent.

Cell Differentiation

Differentiation is the process by which a cell becomes specialised. Although every cell in the body contains the same DNA, different genes are switched on or off in different cell types. This means each specialised cell produces only the proteins needed for its specific function.

The design of specialised cells directly reflects their function. Red blood cells are biconcave discs with no nucleus — this removes the nucleus and increases the surface area for oxygen-carrying haemoglobin. Neurones have long axons that allow electrical impulses to travel over large distances quickly. Root hair cells have long thin extensions that dramatically increase their surface area for absorbing water and mineral ions from the soil.

Sperm cells have a streamlined head containing an acrosome (with enzymes to penetrate the egg), a midpiece packed with mitochondria to supply energy for swimming, and a long flagellum tail for motility. Every feature serves the single purpose of delivering genetic material to an egg.

Muscle cells (muscle fibres) are elongated cells that can shorten and extend. They contain large numbers of mitochondria (for ATP production during contraction) and specialised proteins (actin and myosin) that slide past each other to generate force. Cells with highly specific roles like these are the endpoint of the differentiation process.

Stem Cells: Undifferentiated and Versatile

Stem cells are cells that have not yet differentiated. They retain the ability to divide and produce cells that can become specialised. There are two main types of stem cell relevant to your course: embryonic stem cells and adult stem cells.

Embryonic stem cells are found in the embryo in the first few days after fertilisation. They are described as pluripotent — they can differentiate into any cell type in the body. This makes them potentially very useful for treating diseases caused by cell loss or damage, such as Parkinson’s disease, type 1 diabetes, or spinal cord injury.

Adult stem cells are found in specific tissues, such as bone marrow (which produces blood stem cells that can differentiate into all blood cell types). They are more limited than embryonic stem cells — they can only produce the range of cells relevant to their tissue. Bone marrow transplants, which replace diseased blood stem cells, are an established medical therapy using adult stem cells.

Scientists have developed a technique to take ordinary adult cells (such as skin cells) and “reprogramme” them genetically to behave like embryonic stem cells. These are called induced pluripotent stem cells (iPS cells). Because they can be made from a patient’s own cells, they would avoid the risk of immune rejection and sidestep many of the ethical concerns associated with embryonic stem cells. iPS cell research is an active and rapidly developing field.

Key Fact

Embryonic stem cells are pluripotent — they can become any cell type. Adult stem cells (e.g. bone marrow) can only produce cells of their own tissue type. iPS cells are reprogrammed adult cells that regain pluripotency without using embryos.

The Ethics of Stem Cell Research

Using embryonic stem cells requires destroying a human embryo at an early stage of development (3–5 days old). This raises serious ethical questions. People who hold that human life begins at fertilisation argue that destroying any embryo is morally wrong, regardless of the medical benefits. Others argue that the potential to alleviate suffering for millions of people outweighs concerns about a cluster of cells at such an early stage, which has no consciousness or capacity for pain.

This is a genuine values-based disagreement, not a scientific one. The science can establish what embryonic stem cells are capable of and what risks they carry. But the question of whether they should be used involves moral, religious and philosophical judgements that science alone cannot resolve. Being able to separate these two types of question is itself an important scientific skill — the distinction between an evidence-based claim and a values-based claim.

Even setting ethics aside, stem cell therapy faces practical challenges. Transplanted cells may be rejected by the patient’s immune system, requiring immunosuppressant drugs that leave the patient vulnerable to infection. There is also a risk that undifferentiated stem cells could divide uncontrollably after transplantation, forming tumours. Researchers must demonstrate that transplanted cells differentiate correctly and integrate safely into the host tissue before therapies can be considered safe enough for widespread clinical use.

The risk–benefit framework applied here mirrors wider scientific decision-making: weighing evidence-based risks (immune rejection, tumour formation) against potential benefits (restored function for people with otherwise untreatable conditions) under conditions of uncertainty. This is a classic IaS4 scenario — science provides the risk data, but the decision about acceptable risk involves values as well as evidence.

Key Fact

The ethics of embryonic stem cell use involves values about when human life begins — a question science cannot answer. Practical risks include immune rejection and uncontrolled cell division (tumour risk). iPS cells and adult stem cells partially address both concerns.
before.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Mitosis produces two genetically identical daughter cells and is used for growth and repair. DNA replication occurs in S phase before mitosis begins. Differentiation produces specialised cells by switching genes on or off.
  • Embryonic stem cells are pluripotent (any cell type). Adult stem cells are more limited. iPS cells are reprogrammed adult cells that regain pluripotency without using embryos.
  • Stem cell ethics involve both scientific evidence (risks, capabilities) and values (beliefs about embryonic life). Science can inform but cannot resolve the values-based dimension of the debate.
before.exam_tip_html: In questions about stem cells and ethics, examiners want you to distinguish between scientific arguments (evidence about what stem cells can do, risks of rejection or tumour formation) and values-based arguments (beliefs about when human life begins, moral weight of potential cures). If you merge these, you lose marks. Always name the type of stem cell you are describing — ‘stem cell’ alone is insufficient. For the mitosis misconception: state clearly that DNA replication happens before mitosis, in S phase. Do not say DNA doubles ‘during mitosis’.

practice_questions.text: A student says 'DNA doubles during mitosis.' Explain why this statement is incorrect and give the correct account of when DNA replication occurs.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: The statement is incorrect because DNA replication occurs in S phase, before mitosis begins — not during mitosis itself. During S phase, each chromosome is copied so that there are two identical copies. Mitosis then separates these copies into two new nuclei, producing two daughter cells each with the same DNA as the parent. By the time mitosis starts, the DNA has already been replicated.
Secure: DNA replication is before mitosis (S phase); mitosis separates the copies.
Developing: DNA copies itself before mitosis.
Emerging: The replication happens before.

Ethical case against: using an embryo destroys a potential human life — those who believe life begins at fertilisation hold this is morally wrong. The decision cannot be made on science alone; it requires weighing evidence-based risks against values-based views on embryonic life.

Developing: Scientific argument; ethical argument; limited integration.
Emerging: Describes stem cells and mentions ethics without developing either.

before.content_html:
Why Size Changes Everything

A single-celled organism like an amoeba gets all the oxygen it needs simply by diffusion across its cell surface. No circulatory system required. But a blue whale — the largest animal ever to have lived — needs a massive heart, kilometres of blood vessels, enormous lungs and elaborate exchange surfaces in its intestines. The fundamental reason is mathematics: as organisms grow, their surface area to volume ratio (SA:V) decreases. The volume (and therefore the number of cells needing supplies) grows faster than the surface area available for exchange.

Consider cubes: a 1 cm cube has a surface area of 6 cm2 and a volume of 1 cm3 — SA:V ratio of 6:1. A 2 cm cube has a surface area of 24 cm2 and volume of 8 cm3 — SA:V ratio of only 3:1. A 3 cm cube has SA:V of 2:1. As the cube grows, its surface area–to–volume ratio halves and then halves again. For a large, complex organism, simple diffusion across the body surface cannot supply oxygen and nutrients fast enough to reach every cell.

Key Fact

As organisms get larger, their surface area to volume ratio decreases. This means the surface area available for gas exchange and nutrient uptake is insufficient to supply all the cells by diffusion alone. Large organisms therefore need specialised exchange surfaces and transport systems.

Moving Substances Across Cell Membranes

Cells exchange substances with their surroundings by three mechanisms. Diffusion is the passive net movement of particles down a concentration gradient — from high to low concentration. No energy is needed. Oxygen diffuses into cells for respiration; carbon dioxide and urea diffuse out.

Osmosis is a special case of diffusion involving only water molecules moving through a partially permeable membrane. Water moves from a region of high water concentration (dilute solution) to a region of low water concentration (concentrated solution). This is important in, for example, kidney function and plant cell water regulation.

Active transport moves substances against the concentration gradient — from low to high concentration. This requires energy in the form of ATP from respiration. Root hair cells use active transport to absorb nitrate ions from the soil even when their internal concentration already exceeds that in the soil. Intestinal epithelial cells also use active transport to absorb glucose from the gut lumen into the blood.

The rate of diffusion is increased by: a steeper concentration gradient (greater difference in concentration between the two sides); a larger surface area (more molecules can cross at once); a shorter diffusion distance (thinner membrane means less distance to travel); and a higher temperature (molecules have more kinetic energy and collide more frequently).

These four factors explain the design of every specialised exchange surface in the body: alveoli have a huge surface area, very thin walls and are richly supplied with blood capillaries that maintain a steep gradient. Villi in the small intestine have a large surface area (with microvilli), a thin epithelium and a dense capillary network. Both surfaces are optimised to maximise diffusion rate.

Key Fact

Diffusion and osmosis are passive (no energy). Active transport requires ATP and moves substances against the concentration gradient. All three are essential for supplying cells — the correct mechanism depends on whether the substance moves with or against its gradient.

Specialised Exchange Surfaces

Because large organisms cannot rely on diffusion alone, evolution has produced highly specialised exchange surfaces shared by several structures in the body. All share the same design principles: large surface area, thin walls and a good supply of blood capillaries that maintain steep concentration gradients.

Alveoli are tiny air sacs clustered at the ends of the smallest airways (bronchioles). Each alveolus is surrounded by a dense network of capillaries. Oxygen diffuses from the air in the alveolus, across the single-cell-thick alveolar wall and capillary wall, into the blood. Carbon dioxide diffuses in the opposite direction. The human lungs contain several hundred million alveoli, giving a combined surface area estimated at around 70 m2 in an average adult — roughly the floor area of a studio flat.

In lung diseases such as emphysema (caused primarily by smoking), alveolar walls break down, reducing the total surface area available for gas exchange. This means less oxygen enters the blood, leaving patients breathless even at rest. This clinical context illustrates why the design features of alveoli — surface area, thin wall, blood supply — are so important: any reduction in these factors directly reduces the efficiency of gas exchange.

Villi are finger-like projections that line the small intestine, increasing its surface area enormously. Each villus has a thin epithelium (one cell thick), a dense network of blood capillaries for absorbing glucose and amino acids into the blood, and a lacteal (lymph vessel) for absorbing fatty acids and glycerol. The epithelial cells themselves also have microvilli (tiny projections on their surface) that further multiply the surface area — this folded structure within a folded structure is a striking example of biological design maximising exchange.

The Circulatory System: Delivering and Collecting

Even with efficient exchange surfaces, substances still need to be transported throughout the body. In humans, this is achieved by the double circulatory system: one circuit carries deoxygenated blood from the heart to the lungs for gas exchange (the pulmonary circuit); a second carries oxygenated blood from the heart to all body tissues (the systemic circuit). Having two circuits maintains high blood pressure for efficient delivery.

Arteries carry blood away from the heart at high pressure and have thick, elastic, muscular walls to withstand this. Veins carry blood back to the heart at lower pressure, with thinner walls and valves to prevent backflow. Capillaries are the key exchange vessels: walls just one cell thick allow substances to diffuse efficiently between blood and surrounding tissues.

Key Fact

Capillaries, alveoli and villi all share the same design principle: thin walls (one cell thick), large total surface area and a good blood supply to maintain steep concentration gradients. These features maximise the rate of substance exchange.
before.exam_tip_html: For SA:V ratio questions, always show your working with the formula SA:V and include units (cm2:cm3). When asked to explain why alveoli or villi are efficient exchange surfaces, use all four design features: large surface area, thin wall (short diffusion distance), steep concentration gradient (maintained by blood supply), and moisture (for gas exchange). Missing one feature typically loses a mark. For ‘compare’ questions about diffusion and active transport, the key contrast is energy requirement and direction relative to the concentration gradient.

before.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Homeostasis maintains stable internal conditions using negative feedback: a change is detected, a corrective response is triggered, and the response switches off once the set point is restored.
  • Blood glucose is controlled by insulin (lowers glucose, triggers storage as glycogen) and glucagon (raises glucose, triggers release from glycogen). Failure of this system causes diabetes — Type 1 (no insulin) or Type 2 (insulin resistance).
  • Temperature regulation uses vasodilation and sweating to cool, and vasoconstriction and shivering to warm — all coordinated by the thermoregulatory centre in the brain.

practice_questions.text: A student is given data from glucose tolerance tests on two people. Person A's blood glucose returns to normal within 90 minutes. Person B's blood glucose remains elevated throughout the 120-minute test period. Suggest what condition Person B may have and explain why their blood glucose stays high.

Mastering: Person B likely has diabetes (1); either their pancreas does not produce insulin (Type 1) or their cells are resistant to insulin (Type 2) (1); without effective insulin response, cells do not take up glucose from the blood (1); so blood glucose concentration remains above normal (1).

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the evidence that links a sedentary lifestyle and obesity to the development of Type 2 diabetes. In your answer, consider what the data shows, any limitations in drawing conclusions, and what the evidence does and does not prove.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Evidence — large-scale studies show a correlation between obesity/physical inactivity and higher rates of Type 2 diabetes (1); biological mechanism — excess fat may reduce insulin sensitivity in cells (1). Limitations — correlation does not prove causation (1); genetic factors also contribute (1); lifestyle changes can reduce risk but not all obese people develop diabetes (1). Balanced evaluative conclusion acknowledging the strength of the evidence alongside its limits (1).
Secure: Discusses evidence and at least one limitation with some evaluation (4–5).
Developing: Describes the link without engaging with evidence quality (2–3).
Emerging: Vague factual statements only (1).

before.content_html:
The Menstrual Cycle

The menstrual cycle prepares the female body for potential pregnancy each month. It is controlled by four interacting hormones that form a complex feedback system. Understanding the timing and role of each hormone is essential for explaining contraception and fertility treatment.

The four hormones and their roles: FSH (follicle-stimulating hormone) is produced by the pituitary gland and stimulates the maturation of an egg inside a follicle in the ovary. As the follicle matures, it produces oestrogen. Oestrogen has three effects: it causes the uterus lining to thicken and repair after menstruation, it inhibits further FSH production (negative feedback), and it stimulates a surge of LH. The LH surge (around day 14 of the cycle) triggers ovulation — the release of the mature egg from the ovary. After ovulation, the empty follicle (now called the corpus luteum) produces progesterone, which maintains the thickened uterus lining ready for implantation. If fertilisation does not occur, progesterone levels drop, the lining breaks down, and menstruation begins, restarting the cycle.

Key Fact

FSH stimulates egg maturation → oestrogen thickens uterus lining and triggers LH surge → LH causes ovulation → progesterone maintains lining. If no pregnancy, progesterone drops → menstruation begins.

Hormonal methods of contraception include the combined pill (containing synthetic oestrogen and progesterone), the progesterone-only mini-pill, implants and injections. These work by maintaining artificially high levels of these hormones, which inhibit FSH production from the pituitary gland. Without FSH, no egg matures, so ovulation does not occur. Hormonal methods are highly effective but can have side effects including headaches and, rarely, increased risk of blood clots.

Non-hormonal methods include condoms (a barrier method that prevents sperm reaching the egg and also protects against sexually transmitted infections), diaphragms (placed over the cervix), copper IUDs (create an environment hostile to sperm), and surgical sterilisation (permanent). When evaluating contraceptive methods, consider effectiveness, reversibility, protection against infections, side effects and convenience — the right choice depends on individual circumstances.

Some people have difficulty conceiving naturally. Fertility treatments use hormones to assist. FSH injections can stimulate ovulation in women whose pituitary gland does not produce sufficient FSH naturally — this is called ovulation induction.

In vitro fertilisation (IVF) is a more complex treatment. FSH is used to stimulate the ovaries to produce several eggs at once. These are collected surgically and fertilised with sperm in a laboratory dish. The embryos are allowed to develop for a few days before one or two are transferred into the uterus. IVF raises important questions about balancing benefits (allowing parenthood for those who cannot conceive naturally) against risks (physical and emotional demands on the patient, the fate of unused embryos) and costs. This kind of risk–benefit reasoning under uncertainty is at the heart of how science informs medical decisions.

When Organs and Control Systems Fail

When key organs fail, medical technology can take over their function — but there are always trade-offs between different treatments. The kidney is a good example. Healthy kidneys filter the blood and remove waste products (especially urea), maintain ion balance and regulate water content. When kidneys fail, waste products accumulate to life-threatening levels.

Two main approaches exist for treating kidney failure. Dialysis uses a machine to filter the blood artificially. Blood flows from the patient through a membrane into a dialysate solution; waste products (urea, excess ions) move across the membrane by diffusion into the solution, while needed substances remain in the blood. Dialysis must be done regularly — typically several sessions a week, each lasting several hours. This places a significant burden on the patient’s time and quality of life, but it does not require surgery and can be maintained long-term.

Kidney transplant involves receiving a healthy kidney from a donor (either a living donor or a recently deceased donor). A successful transplant restores full kidney function and frees the patient from dialysis. However, the patient must take immunosuppressant drugs for life to prevent the immune system from rejecting the donated organ. These drugs increase the risk of infections and other complications. Donors and recipients must be carefully matched to reduce rejection risk, and there are far fewer kidneys available than patients who need them.

Key Fact

Dialysis filters blood artificially — regular sessions required, no surgery, sustainable long-term. Kidney transplant restores full function but requires lifelong immunosuppressants and depends on donor availability. The decision between them involves weighing clinical, personal and logistical factors.

The kidney is not the only organ that can fail. Heart failure can be managed with medication, mechanical assist devices, or — in severe cases — a heart transplant. Liver failure may require a liver transplant (the liver can partially regenerate, so living donors can donate a segment). Pancreatic beta cell failure (Type 1 diabetes) is managed with insulin replacement rather than organ transplant, though research into islet cell transplantation is ongoing. In every case, the principles are the same: understand what function has been lost, weigh the available interventions, and consider both the benefits and the risks for the individual patient.
before.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The menstrual cycle is controlled by FSH, LH, oestrogen and progesterone in a feedback loop. FSH matures the egg; oestrogen thickens the lining and triggers the LH surge; LH causes ovulation; progesterone maintains the lining.
  • Hormonal contraception inhibits FSH, preventing ovulation. IVF uses FSH to stimulate multiple egg production and raises ethical questions about benefits, risks and the fate of unused embryos.
  • When organs fail, treatments aim to replace lost function. Kidney failure can be managed with dialysis (regular, no surgery) or transplant (full function restored but requires immunosuppressants and donor availability).

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the decision to use IVF as a fertility treatment. In your answer, consider the scientific, personal and ethical dimensions of the decision. Reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Scientific benefits — effective for some causes of infertility; uses FSH to increase egg production; success rates improving (1). Personal benefits — allows people who cannot conceive naturally to have children; significant emotional value (1). Scientific risks — hormone treatment has side effects; multiple pregnancy risk if more than one embryo implanted (1). Ethical concerns — unused embryos are destroyed or remain stored; some people view these as potential lives (1). Conclusion addresses whether benefits outweigh concerns, acknowledging that the answer depends on individual values and circumstances — not purely a scientific question (1). Quality of reasoning sustained throughout (1).
